(CNN) --     More than 5,000 patients of a South Dakota urology clinic may have been exposed to hepatitis and HIV when the facility reused single-use medical products, state health officials said Friday. Clinic workers told inspectors they've been reusing products since the clinic opened its doors in 2002. The Siouxland Urology Center in Dakota Dunes has been ordered to contact nearly 5,700 former patients treated there since 2002. A routine inspection found the facility was reusing sterile saline bags, tubing and other medical supplies from cystoscopies -- a diagnostic procedure that looks at the lower urinary tract. "We witnessed the practice while we were in the facility," during a January inspection, said Barb Buhler of the South Dakota Health Department. Siouxland Urology has since been put under a provisional license and has been very cooperative, according to state officials. "Siouxland Urology Center informed certain of its patients by U.S. mail that a prior cystoscopy procedure could have potentially exposed them to an infectious disease," the facility's Web site said. It added that "the risk of infection from our past procedure is very minimal and we are unaware of any blood infections in our patients caused by the cystoscopy practice." The clinic, which primarily serves clients from South Dakota, Iowa and Nebraska, is offering free blood tests to those possibly affected to rule out the presence of viruses .Watch more on the possible exposure of urology patients » . On January 21, South Dakota Department of Health inspectors entered an examining room where a cystoscopy was about to take place, and noticed that a saline bag, which was hanging on a pole, was dated January 19, said Bob Stahl, of the South Dakota Department of Health. The inspectors, who are registered nurses, questioned the clinic staff. The clinic staff said they routinely reused saline bags and tubing, although both are clearly marked "for single use only," Stahl said. "They used the bags and tubing on multiple patients," Stahl said. He said the workers at the clinic told the inspectors they'd been reusing bags and tubing since the clinic opened in 2002. They said they didn't see anything wrong with the practice, Stahl said. "It was their standard operating procedure," Stahl said. "They told the inspectors that this was a common practice all over the country. We disagreed and told them this was not a common practice." He said that the clinic had been inspected seven times since it opened, and no one had noticed that the clinic was reusing equipment. "It was just by chance that this saline bag was hanging there. We run across these things by luck at times," Stahl said. "We're fortunate that the team was able to identify this." Fluids from patients can retreat into saline bags and tubing while the equipment is used, and reusing the tubing or saline bags could put patients at risk for contacting diseases from previous patients. A 1-liter bag of saline and tubing costs about $4, according to Mary Jo Lallis, account manager for PSS World Medical, Inc., a medical supply company. CNN's Greg Morrison and Elizabeth Cohen contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN** — South Dakota health officials are urging thousands of patients to get tested for bloodborne infections after an investigation revealed a local urology clinic repeatedly reused single-use medical equipment, potentially exposing patients to hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

The South Dakota Department of Health (SDDOH) announced the warning on Tuesday following an unannounced audit of the Prairie State Urology Center in Sioux Falls. According to state investigators, the clinic had been improperly cleaning and reusing devices specifically manufactured and labeled for single use during invasive procedures, including prostate biopsies and cystoscopies.

Officials estimate that as many as 3,500 patients who underwent procedures at the facility between January 2019 and last month may have been exposed.

"This is a severe breach of basic infection control standards," South Dakota Secretary of Health Melissa Magstadt said during a news conference. "While the risk of actual infection transmission to any individual patient remains low, the failure to follow proper medical protocols is unacceptable. We are taking immediate steps to ensure all affected individuals are notified and offered testing."

### A 'Lapse in Protocol'

The investigation was triggered in late October after a clinic employee filed a complaint with state health authorities, alleging that staff members were instructed to sterilize and reuse single-use equipment—including plastic tubing, guide needles, and fluid bags—to cut costs. 

Single-use medical devices are designed by manufacturers for a single procedure on a single patient because their design makes thorough cleaning and sterilization virtually impossible. Reusing them poses a significant risk of cross-contamination.

In a statement released late Tuesday, Prairie State Urology Center said it had suspended operations and was fully cooperating with state and federal authorities. 

"We are deeply saddened and apologetic for the distress this situation causes our patients and their families," the clinic said. "We have initiated a comprehensive internal review, terminated the individuals directly responsible for supervising these infection control protocols, and are working around the clock to assist public health officials."

### Patients Left Reeling

The health department began mailing certified notification letters to affected patients on Wednesday. The state has set up dedicated testing sites in Sioux Falls, Rapid City, and Pierre, offering free blood screenings for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV to anyone who received a letter.

For patients, the news has caused profound anxiety. 

"You trust that when you go into a doctor's office, the equipment being used on you is clean and safe," said Mark Henderson, 62, who underwent a prostate biopsy at the clinic in 2022. "To get a letter saying you need to be tested for HIV because a doctor wanted to save a few bucks on plastic tubing is horrifying."

Attorneys representing several patients have already announced plans to file a class-action lawsuit against the clinic and its primary operators, alleging gross negligence and medical malpractice.

### Understanding the Risks

Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV are bloodborne viruses that can cause severe, long-term health complications if left untreated. While HIV attacks the body's immune system, hepatitis B and C affect the liver and can lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer. 

Infectious disease experts emphasize that while the potential for transmission exists, these viruses do not survive easily on exposed surfaces, meaning the actual rate of transmission may prove to be low.

"The risk varies depending on the specific device, how it was sanitized between uses, and the viral load of any infected patient," said Dr. Sanjay Gupta, CNN Chief Medical Correspondent. "However, because hepatitis C and HIV can remain asymptomatic for years, testing is critical to catch any potential infections early when treatments are most effective."

State health officials said no confirmed cases of infection have yet been directly linked to the clinic, though results from patient screenings are expected to roll in over the coming weeks.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have joined the investigation. State regulators indicated that the clinic's medical licenses remain under review and could be permanently revoked.

**DAKOTA DUNES, S.D.** — State health inspectors have uncovered a massive, decades-long breach of infection control protocols at a local medical facility, revealing that staff had been systematically reusing $4 single-use IV saline bags on surgical patients for more than 20 years.

According to a scathing report released Tuesday by the South Dakota Department of Health, the practice took place during outpatient cystoscopy procedures—invasive examinations used to inspect the bladder and urethra—dating back to 2002. 

Inspectors discovered that instead of discarding the intravenous saline bags after flushing the bladder of a single patient, as mandated by federal safety guidelines and manufacturer warnings, clinic staff routinely left the bags hanging to use on subsequent patients, merely changing the outer tubing. 

The low-cost bags, which retail for approximately $4 each, are clearly labeled by manufacturers and the FDA as "Single-Use Only" due to the high risk of fluid backflow and cross-contamination.

The systemic failure was uncovered last month during an unannounced, routine inspection of the facility. According to the state report, an inspector observed a nurse using a half-empty bag of saline on a patient that had already been connected to a previous patient's catheter. When questioned, staff members reportedly admitted that reusing the bags was a "standard cost-saving measure" that had been passed down through training protocols since 2002.

Health officials estimate that thousands of patients who underwent cystoscopies at the Dakota Dunes facility over the past 22 years may have been exposed to serious blood-borne pathogens and bacterial infections, including Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV, and severe urinary tract infections.

"The willingness to compromise patient safety to save four dollars on a single-use plastic bag is an appalling violation of the medical oath," said Dr. Ellen Vance, an infectious disease specialist and patient safety advocate not affiliated with the investigation. "Cystoscopy involves direct contact with mucosal tissue. Reusing irrigation fluids creates a direct pipeline for cross-patient contamination."

In response to the findings, the South Dakota Department of Health immediately suspended the facility’s operating license for surgical procedures and issued a public health mandate requiring the clinic to notify all patients who underwent a cystoscopy at the location between January 2002 and the present.

The state is establishing a dedicated hotline and offering free blood testing and medical consultations for affected patients.

In a brief written statement issued late Tuesday, the management of the Dakota Dunes facility expressed "profound regret" over the breach.

"We are shocked and deeply saddened by these findings," the statement read. "This practice was a grave departure from our core values and standards of care. We are cooperating fully with state regulators, have placed the clinic's administrative leadership on administrative leave, and are committed to reaching out to every impacted patient."

State law enforcement and the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office have been notified of the findings to determine whether criminal charges or regulatory fines will be filed against the facility or individual staff members.

State health officials are urging anyone who underwent a urological procedure in Dakota Dunes within the last 22 years to contact their primary care physician or call the state's dedicated patient help line. The investigation remains ongoing.

**STATE HEALTH DEPARTMENT ISSUES URGENT ALERT AFTER CLINIC REUSED TUBING AND SALINE BAGS ON OVER 1,200 PATIENTS**

**FAIRFIELD, Mass.** — State health authorities have launched a sweeping investigation into the Oakwood Outpatient Urology Center following revelations that clinical staff systematically reused single-use medical tubing and fluid bags during routine cystoscopy procedures, potentially exposing more than 1,200 patients to bloodborne pathogens and severe bacterial infections.

The breach, which state inspectors say persisted for nearly nine months, involved the fluid irrigation systems used during cystoscopies—a common procedure where a thin, lighted tube is inserted through the urethra to examine the bladder. 

According to an emergency order issued Thursday by the Massachusetts Department of Public Health (DPH), staff at the facility routinely failed to replace the IV saline bags and primary fluid delivery tubing between patients. Instead, clinicians changed only the small catheter tips that directly touched the patient, leaving the main fluid lines and intravenous bags connected for multiple consecutive procedures throughout the day.

Public health experts warn that fluid backflow into the tubing creates a significant risk of cross-contamination, exposing subsequent patients to blood, tissue, and bodily fluids from previous procedures. 

"This represents a fundamental, unacceptable breakdown of basic infection control protocols," said Dr. Aris Thorne, Chief Medical Officer at the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. "While the statistical risk of viral transmission in any single patient may be low, the sheer volume of individuals subjected to this practice over an extended period turns this into a major public health intervention. Single-use devices are designated as such for a reason—reusing them compromises the sterile field entirely."

The DPH immediately suspended the clinic’s license to perform invasive urological procedures on Monday following an unannounced audit. The inspection was triggered by an internal whistleblower—a newly hired surgical technician who noticed the practice and alerted state regulators last week.

Investigators found that the protocol was not an isolated mistake by a single employee, but a standardized clinic workflow driven by a misunderstanding of equipment guidelines and attempts to reduce turnover time between patients.

"Our regulatory teams discovered an informal internal guidance document at the facility that falsely claimed one-way check valves made it safe to reuse primary irrigation lines across multiple patients," said Elena Rostova, Director of the DPH Bureau of Health Care Safety and Quality. "That guidance directly contradicts federal standards set by the FDA and CDC. A check valve is not an absolute barrier against microscopic pathogens, and it does not replace the requirement for a completely sterile setup for every single patient."

The state has ordered Oakwood Health Network, the parent organization operating the clinic, to immediately notify 1,240 patients who underwent a cystoscopy at the facility between January 12 and September 30 of this year. 

The health department is advising all affected patients to undergo screening for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Additionally, the state is monitoring local emergency rooms for any spike in antibiotic-resistant urinary tract infections or urosepsis linked to the clinic.

Oakwood Health Network issued a statement late Thursday offering a "profound apology" to affected patients and confirmed that the clinic’s medical director and nurse manager have been placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the state investigation. The health network has established a dedicated hotline and promised to cover all costs associated with blood testing and follow-up care for impacted patients.

Health officials emphasized that no confirmed cases of infection transmission have been definitively linked to the breach yet, though full blood screening results could take weeks to process. 

"We understand the intense anxiety this news causes for patients and their families," Dr. Thorne added. "Our immediate priority is ensuring every affected individual receives free, confidential testing and appropriate medical counseling. Simultaneously, we are conducting a comprehensive review of all ambulatory surgical centers in the region to ensure that these reckless shortcuts are not occurring anywhere else."

The state DPH indicated that its investigation remains ongoing, and the results will be forwarded to the State Attorney General’s office to determine whether administrative fines or further regulatory penalties are warranted.

The clinic faced intense public scrutiny and legal action after it was revealed that nearly 3,000 patients had been potentially exposed to bloodborne pathogens, including **HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C**, due to improper medical equipment sterilization practices.

Here is a breakdown of the story as reported by CNN and other major news organizations at the time:

---

### **1. The Cause of the Breach**
The issue centered on procedures involving **prostate biopsies**. According to reports and health department investigations:
* Staff at Siouxland Urology had been reusing **single-use needle guides**—devices attached to ultrasound probes used during prostate biopsies.
* Manufacturer guidelines and federal regulations strictly mandated that these guides be used once and disposed of to prevent cross-contamination between patients.
* The practice of reusing these single-use parts reportedly occurred over a four-year period, from **2009 to early 2013**.

### **2. The Scope and Patient Notification**
In June 2013, the clinic began sending letters to approximately **2,800 to 3,000 patients** who had undergone transrectal prostate biopsies at the facility during that timeframe. 

* The letters informed patients that they might have been exposed to infectious diseases, specifically **HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C**.
* Patients were strongly urged to undergo blood testing to check for infection.
* Siouxland Urology offered to pay for the blood tests for affected patients.

### **3. Discovery and Clinic Response**
The breach was discovered internally during an audit or review of medical procedures. 
* Once the error was identified, the clinic stated that it immediately corrected the process, switched to proper disposable protocols, and self-reported the incident to the South Dakota Department of Health and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
* Clinic leadership issued public apologies, maintaining that the risk of actual disease transmission was low, but acknowledging that the failure to follow proper procedure was a serious oversight.

### **4. Legal Fallout and Public Reaction**
The announcement caused widespread panic and anger among patients and their families in the Siouxland area.

* **Class-Action Lawsuits:** Multiple patients filed lawsuits against Siouxland Urology, alleging medical negligence, battery, and severe emotional distress caused by the fear of contracting life-altering diseases.
* **Regulatory Oversight:** State health officials and medical boards launched investigations into the facility’s protocols and staff training.

### **5. Aftermath and Health Impact**
While the incident resulted in significant anxiety and legal settlements, follow-up testing of the thousands of notified patients did not yield a massive outbreak of HIV or Hepatitis connected directly to the clinic. However, the scandal served as a prominent national example of the dangers of failing to follow single-use medical device protocols, leading to tighter auditing in outpatient surgical and urology clinics nationwide.

**State Health Department Warns Thousands of Patient Exposure to Bloodborne Pathogens at Local Medical Clinic**

**ALBUQUERQUE, N.M.** — Public health officials are urging more than 3,500 former patients of an Albuquerque-based pain management clinic to undergo testing for bloodborne pathogens after an investigation revealed widespread reuse of single-use medical supplies over a two-year period.

The New Mexico Department of Health (NMDOH) issued an urgent public health notification on Tuesday targeting individuals who received intravenous treatments or joint injections at the High Desert Wellness and Pain Center between January 2022 and December 2023. 

According to state regulators, the clinic engaged in unsafe infection control practices, including the reuse of single-use syringes and the re-entering of single-dose medication vials to treat multiple patients. The breaches significantly heighten the risk of transmission for bloodborne infections, including Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).

"Invasive procedures require strict adherence to infection control standards. The practices uncovered at this facility represent a serious violation of basic medical protocols and patient trust," said Dr. Laura Reyes, Deputy State Epidemiologist, during a news conference Tuesday afternoon. "While we have not yet confirmed any direct transmissions tied to the clinic, the sheer volume of potential exposures mandates immediate, large-scale screening."

The investigation began in late November following a tip from a former clinical employee who raised concerns with the New Mexico Medical Board. State inspectors conducted an unannounced site visit shortly thereafter, reporting observed instances of compromised supply sterility, lack of proper auto-cleaving equipment, and improper disposal of hazardous biological waste.

In December, state health officials issued an emergency suspension of the clinic's operating license and ordered its primary practitioner, Dr. Arthur Vance, to cease practicing medicine pending a formal administrative hearing.

According to documents released by the NMDOH, clinic staff allegedly reused syringes to administer saline flushes and injected multiple patients using single-dose vials of corticosteroid and anesthetic medications. Single-dose vials do not contain preservatives; once accessed, they can easily become contaminated with bacteria or viruses and spread infection if used on subsequent patients.

Efforts to reach Dr. Vance or legal counsel representing High Desert Wellness and Pain Center were not immediately successful. A voice message left at the clinic’s main phone line informed callers that the office was "closed indefinitely."

The state has begun mailing notification letters directly to affected patients identified through clinic billing records. Health authorities are offering free blood testing for Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV at county health offices throughout the state. A dedicated hotline has also been established to assist concerned patients in scheduling appointments and navigating potential medical follow-up.

Medical experts emphasize that bloodborne diseases often show no initial symptoms, making laboratory testing crucial for early detection and treatment. 

"Many people infected with Hepatitis C or HIV can go years without feeling sick, even while damage to the liver or immune system is occurring," Dr. Reyes said. "We strongly advise anyone who received an injection at this facility during the specified timeframe to get tested as soon as possible."

The state licensing board’s disciplinary hearing regarding Dr. Vance’s medical license is scheduled for next month. State prosecutors declined to comment on whether criminal charges are being considered.
